prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The crocodile, with cunning smile, sat in the dentist’s chair. He said, “Right here and everywhere my teeth require repair.” The dentist’s face was turning white. He quivered, quaked and shook. He muttered, “I suppose I’m going to have to take a look.” “I want you”, Crocodile declared, “to do the back ones first. The molars at the very back are easily the worst.” He opened wide his massive jaws. It was a fearsome sight— At least three hundred pointed teeth, all sharp and shining white. The dentist kept himself well clear. He stood two yards away. He chose the longest probe he had to search out the decay. “I said to do the back ones first!” the Crocodile called out. “You’re much too far away, dear sir, to see what you’re about. To do the back ones properly you’ve got to put your head Deep down inside my great big mouth,” the grinning Crocky said. The poor old dentist wrung his hands and, weeping in despair, He cried, “No no! I see them all extremely well from here!” Just then, in burst a lady, in her hands a golden chain. She cried, “Oh Croc, you naughty boy, you’re playing tricks again!” “Watch out!” the dentist shrieked and started climbing up the wall. “He’s after me! He’s after you! He’s going to eat us all!” “Don’t be a twit,” the lady said, and flashed a gorgeous smile. “He’s harmless. He’s my little pet, my lovely crocodile.”

outputs.L1:
The crocodile, wearing a cunning smile, sat in the dentist’s chair.

“Right here—and everywhere—my teeth require repair,” he said.

The dentist’s face turned pale. He trembled, quivered, and shook. “I suppose,” he muttered, “I shall have to take a look.”

“I want you,” the Crocodile declared, “to begin with the back ones. The molars at the very back are easily the worst.”

He opened his massive jaws wide. It was a fearsome sight: at least three hundred pointed teeth, all sharp and gleaming white.

The dentist kept well clear, standing two yards away. He selected the longest probe he had to search for decay.

“I said to do the back ones first!” the Crocodile called out. “You are much too far away, dear sir, to see what you are doing. To do the back ones properly, you must put your head deep down inside my great big mouth,” the grinning Crocky said.

The poor old dentist wrung his hands and, weeping in despair, cried, “No, no! I can see them all extremely well from here!”

Just then, a lady burst in, a golden chain in her hands.

“Oh, Croc, you naughty boy,” she cried. “You are playing tricks again!”

“Watch out!” the dentist shrieked, and began climbing up the wall. “He is after me! He is after you! He is going to eat us all!”

“Do not be a twit,” the lady said, flashing a gorgeous smile. “He is harmless. He is my little pet, my lovely crocodile.”
outputs.L2:
A crocodile wearing a sly grin settled into the dentist’s chair. He announced, “My teeth need fixing—this spot, that spot, in fact all over.”

The dentist went pale. Trembling from head to foot, he murmured, “I suppose I’ll have to examine them.”

“I want you to begin with the teeth right at the back,” said the crocodile. “The rear molars are in the worst condition.”

Then he stretched open his enormous mouth. It was terrifying to see: at least three hundred gleaming white teeth, each one sharp and pointed.

The dentist made sure to keep his distance. Standing about two yards away, he picked up the longest dental instrument he owned and tried to check for cavities from afar.

“I told you to start at the back!” the crocodile shouted. “You’re standing far too far away, my good man, to know what you’re doing. If you want to treat those back teeth properly, you’ll need to put your head deep inside my enormous mouth,” he added with a broad grin.

The miserable dentist clasped his hands together and began to cry in panic. “No, no! I can see everything perfectly well from here!”

At that moment, a woman rushed into the room carrying a gold chain. “Oh, Croc, you naughty creature!” she exclaimed. “You’re up to your tricks again!”

“Be careful!” screamed the dentist, scrambling up the wall. “He’s trying to get me! He’ll get you too! He means to eat us both!”

“Don’t be silly,” the woman replied, smiling beautifully. “He wouldn’t hurt anyone. He’s my dear little pet—my wonderful crocodile.”
outputs.L3:
A crocodile once visited a dentist and complained that all of his teeth needed repair. He said that every tooth in his mouth hurt and that the dentist would have to examine them carefully.

When the crocodile opened his enormous mouth, the dentist was terrified. Inside were rows of long, sharp teeth, and the dentist could not stop imagining what might happen if the jaws suddenly snapped shut.

The crocodile then insisted that the dentist must put his head deep inside his mouth to examine the back teeth properly. He opened his mouth even wider and told the dentist not to be afraid.

However, the frightened dentist refused. Instead, he tried to look at the crocodile’s teeth from a safe distance, stretching his neck and holding his tools as far away as possible. He was far too nervous to go anywhere near the crocodile’s dangerous-looking jaws.

Just then, a lady arrived and calmly explained the situation. She said that the crocodile was only playing tricks on the dentist and that he was actually her harmless pet. The dentist was relieved, though he was still not eager to put his head inside the crocodile’s mouth.
outputs.L4:
A crocodile came to see the dentist one bright morning, and from the moment he entered the office, everyone was frightened. His long green body filled the doorway, his heavy tail dragged across the floor, and his mouth was lined with rows of sharp white teeth. The dentist, trembling behind his chair, asked what the problem was.

The crocodile opened his jaws very wide and said politely that several of his teeth were hurting and needed to be repaired. The dentist tried to look brave, but the sight of that enormous mouth made his knees shake. He picked up his mirror and tools, leaned forward carefully, and began to examine the crocodile’s front teeth.

“Farther back, please,” said the crocodile.

The dentist swallowed hard and took one small step closer. He checked another tooth and hoped the visit would soon be over.

“No, no,” the crocodile insisted. “The trouble is with the molars at the very back. You must put your head right inside and take a proper look.”

The dentist became more terrified than ever. He imagined the great jaws snapping shut while he was leaning inside. Still, the crocodile kept urging him to look deeper and deeper into his mouth. The dentist’s hands shook, and he could barely hold his instruments. He leaned in a little, then pulled back. The crocodile opened wider and waited.

Just as the dentist thought he could not bear another moment, a woman rushed into the room. She called the crocodile by name and scolded him for frightening the poor dentist. Then she explained that the crocodile was her pet and was not dangerous at all. He had only been teasing, pretending to be fierce while asking for dental treatment.

The dentist, still pale and nervous, slowly realized that he had not been in real danger. The crocodile was harmless, and the terrible situation had been a comic misunderstanding. What had seemed like a terrifying visit from a hungry beast turned out to be nothing more than a naughty pet playing a trick on a very frightened dentist.
outputs.L5:
**The Right Crocodile**

In the heart of a wide green swamp lived a crocodile who was known by everyone as **The Right Crocodile**. He did not get this name because he was always correct, or because he never made mistakes. He earned it because he always tried to do the right thing.

While other crocodiles snapped at anything that moved, The Right Crocodile was careful and thoughtful. He helped small birds find safe branches, guided lost turtles back to the river, and warned young animals when storms were coming. Many creatures were afraid of crocodiles, but they soon learned that this one was different.

One day, a little monkey dropped a basket of fruit into the water. The current carried it straight toward the deepest part of the swamp. The monkey cried from the shore, sure that everything was lost. The Right Crocodile swam slowly forward, lifted the basket gently on his back, and returned it without taking even a single mango.

“Why did you help me?” asked the monkey.

The crocodile smiled. “Because it was the right thing to do.”

From that day on, the animals remembered an important lesson: being strong does not mean being cruel. True strength is knowing when to be kind, when to be fair, and when to help others. And in that swamp, no one forgot the name of **The Right Crocodile**.

counterfactuals.output:
The crocodile came in at two,  
With jaws as wide as gates,  
He said, “Dear dentist, do be quick—  
I’ve quite important dates!”  

The dentist peeked, then gave a squeak,  
And trembled in his seat:  
“For in that grin, from end to end,  
Are three hundred shining teeth!”  

He brushed the left, he brushed the right,  
He polished every row,  
While crocodile smiled sweetly and said,  
“Do mind the ones below.”  

The dentist tied a looking-glass  
Upon a silver string,  
Then dropped it down the crocodile—  
And heard it faintly ring!  

“Oh dear!” he cried. “Oh my!” he cried.  
“This job is far too wide!”  
The crocodile said, “Don’t be scared—  
I only bite outside.”  

At last each tooth was clean and bright,  
As sharp as pins could be;  
The dentist bowed, then backed away  
And climbed a nearby tree.  

The crocodile paid three gold coins  
And waved a fond goodbye:  
“I’ll come again next Tuesday noon!”  
The dentist said, “Oh my!”
